# APA redline — Brightline Cabinetry / Lone Star Millwork (seller's markup of buyer draft)

**Working assumptions (prominent, per engagement rules):**
- **Purchase Price is not stated in the draft excerpt.** Escrow §9.3 says "$310,000 (10%)", implying a Purchase Price of **$310,000 ÷ 0.10 = $3,100,000**. All dollar caps below use that figure. Confirm actual price and allocation (QUESTIONS.md Q1).
- Payroll-tax rates used below (employer FICA 7.65%; FUTA 0.6% on first $7,000/employee) are **not in the library and are unverified**; the library establishes that the liability categories exist and that §3509 reduced rates apply if non-willful (`worker_classification_tx_irs.md`).
- Every citation below is to a file listed in `library/INDEX.md`; anything else is labeled unverified.

---

## §2.4 Earn-Out — **CHANGE (mechanics and economics)**

**Proposed language (replaces the EBITDA sentence; new (b)-(e) added):**

> "EBITDA" means, for the Measurement Period, the earnings of the Business before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, determined in accordance with GAAP applied on a basis consistent with Seller's accounting principles, methods and practices as used in the 2025 management accounts, consistently applied throughout the Measurement Period, and without giving effect to: (i) allocations of Buyer's or its Affiliates' corporate overhead, management fees or shared-services charges; (ii) transaction, financing, integration, synergy-capture, restructuring and purchase-accounting charges, and any accounting changes required by the Transaction; and (iii) costs of expanding the Business beyond its operation as of Closing.
> (b) From Closing through the Measurement Period, Buyer shall operate the Business in the ordinary course consistent with past practice and shall not take any action, or omit to take any action, the purpose or effect of which is to reduce or avoid the Earn-Out, including diverting customers, orders or revenues to any business of Buyer or its Affiliates.
> (c) Buyer shall deliver to Seller, within 45 days after each of the first four fiscal quarters, an unaudited statement of the Business's EBITDA. Seller may, on reasonable notice, audit through an independent accounting firm of its selection at Seller's expense.
> (d) Any dispute over EBITDA shall be referred, exclusively and finally, to a nationally recognized independent accounting firm jointly selected by the parties; its determination governs; its fees are allocated in inverse proportion to the degree it sustains each party's position.
> (e) If Buyer sells the Business or substantially all of its assets or equity during the Measurement Period, the maximum Earn-Out amount becomes immediately due and payable at the time of that sale.

**Why.** "As determined by Buyer in good faith in accordance with Buyer's accounting policies" lets the buyer allocate overhead, management fees, integration costs and purchase-accounting adjustments against the Business and zero the earn-out; the practice-note protections are exactly the list above (`earnout_definitions.md`; *Lazard Technology Partners v. Qinetiq*, 114 A.3d 193 (Del. 2015)). **Economics, shown:** threshold $700,000; 2025 EBITDA $740k (seller-prepared) pays 0.40 × (740,000 − 700,000) = **$16,000**; full $400,000 requires EBITDA of 700,000 + 400,000 ÷ 0.40 = **$1,700,000** (~2.3× current); EBITDA net of the disclosed add-backs (740,000 − 180,000 owner salary − 42,000 legal = $518,000) pays **$0**. As drafted the earn-out is close to worthless. Negotiation: either lower the threshold or convert the earn-out headline into the fixed Closing Payment. Do not let the buyer bank the $400k "contingent consideration" while paying nothing.

## §3.3 / Schedule 3.3 Required Consents — **CHANGE (schedule is false as drafted)**

**Proposed Schedule 3.3 (replaces "None."):**

> 1. Hensley Homes Master Supply Agreement §18 — consent, may be withheld in sole discretion. Seller to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain written consent prior to Closing.
> 2. Shop Lease (7700 Burleson Rd) §22 — landlord consent to assignment, not to be unreasonably withheld. Seller to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain written consent prior to Closing.

**And add a closing condition (Article VII):**

> Receipt of the written consents listed on Schedule 3.3, in each case without modification of the underlying contract's economic terms; provided that if Hensley Homes conditions its consent on modified commercial terms, the parties shall in good faith consider a corresponding purchase-price adjustment, and either party may decline to close on that basis.

**Why.** A clause barring assignment "by operation of law, merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise" is enforced as written; the unconsented asset-sale transfer is a breach and the transfer **void** (`anti_assignment_change_of_control.md`: *SQL Solutions v. Oracle*, 1991 WL 626458 (N.D. Cal.); Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§317, 322). Hensley is 38% of revenue and consent is in its "sole discretion," which the library notes is leverage to renegotiate price. Keeping the risk allocation seller-protective: the condition is **mutual** and tied to *unmodified* terms, so the buyer cannot use Hensley's response as a walk-away/reprice option. Cascade Builders (§1.2) needs **notice only** — put it on a notice schedule as a closing deliverable. The 22 residential contracts are silent: rights are generally assignable; obligations need consent only where performance is personal (Restatement §§317, 322) — notice/novation, no condition.

## §4.12 Employees and Contractors — **CHANGE (cannot sign clean; Ray knows)**

**Proposed language (replaces §4.12; pairs with §7.4(b) below):**

> 4.12 Employees and Contractors. Except as set forth on Schedule 4.12, all individuals providing services to the Business have been classified as employees or independent contractors as required by applicable law, and Seller has withheld, remitted and paid all employment, payroll and withholding taxes required to have been withheld or paid. **Schedule 4.12** shall disclose, at a minimum: the nine installers paid on Form 1099 (exclusive service, Seller-provided trucks and tools, daily scheduling by the shop foreman, hourly rates of $34-41, average tenure 3.4 years, no written agreements), the Hardaway Builders dispute, and the open warranty log.
> 4.12A Classification Special Indemnity. Seller shall indemnify Buyer for Losses arising from employment-tax assessments or wage-and-hour claims relating to the individuals disclosed on Schedule 4.12, in each case only for services rendered prior to Closing, subject to a cap of **$[150,000-200,000]** (sizing below), with no Basket applying, surviving until 60 days after expiration of the applicable limitations period. Such Losses shall not count toward the Basket or the §7.4(b) Cap, and Buyer shall not bring a §7.1 claim in respect of the disclosed arrangement itself.

**Why.** The nine installers "work exclusively for one business, on its schedule, with its tools and vehicles, paid hourly, for years" — the library's own facts pattern: **employees under the common-law control test regardless of label** (IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41; Treas. Reg. §31.3121(d)-1; `worker_classification_tx_irs.md`). A clean rep Ray knows to be false is both a sandbagged indemnity and a fraud risk (see §7.4(c) below). The library's seller protections apply verbatim: disclose, then size a special indemnity (`sandbagging.md`). **Sizing, shown:** $612,000 × 7.65% = $46,818/yr employer FICA; FUTA 0.6% × $7,000 × 9 = $378/yr; ≈ **$47.2k/yr**; average tenure 3.4 yrs → ~3 years ≈ **$141.6k**; plus overtime (hours unknown — QUESTIONS.md Q2), any years before the 3.4-yr average, and interest/penalties (rates/periods not in the library — unverified, left open). Section 3509 reduced rates should cut the FICA/FUTA component if non-willful (`worker_classification_tx_irs.md`; rates themselves not in library — unverified). Hence a **$150k-200k** proposed cap, to be refined when Q1-Q3 answers land. Texas UI successor provisions are the buyer's reason to *want* this structure (Tex. Lab. Code §201.041; 40 TAC §815.134; successor FLSA risk with substantial continuity, per the same library file) — the buyer's reclassification need is a pricing conversation, not a seller-rep conversation.

## §7.4(a) Basket — **KEEP**

Deductible (not tipping) at $75,000 is seller-favorable and market-consistent as a structure (ABA Deal Points Study — `baskets_caps.md`); $75,000 ÷ $3,100,000 ≈ **2.4%** of price. Known items (warranty $23,000 + Hardaway $9,800 = $32,800) stay under it. If the buyer proposes tipping or a below-basket "mini-basket" for the special indemnity, hold the line: the special indemnity already has no basket, which is its concession.

## §7.4(b) Cap — **CHANGE one carve-out**

**Proposed language (replaces the exception clause):**

> ...except for Fundamental Representations, which shall be subject to a cap equal to the Purchase Price. Losses under §4.12A are subject solely to the Classification Cap.

**Why.** Keep general cap 10% of price (= $310,000, matching escrow) and fundamental reps at full price — both market (ABA Deal Points Study — `baskets_caps.md`). But carving the **operational** worker-classification rep out to a full-Purchase-Price cap "is off-market and should be resisted or replaced with a sized special indemnity" (`baskets_caps.md`, near-verbatim). As drafted Ray carries up to $3.1M against a ~$47k/yr problem. Delete "Section 4.12" from the exception; move classification to the §4.12A special indemnity.

## §7.4(c) Sandbagging — **CHANGE (reject as drafted)**

Buyer's counsel called this "market-standard knowledge language." It is the opposite: it is a **pro-sandbagging** clause — buyer keeps indemnity rights "regardless of knowledge acquired (or capable of being acquired) ... before or after execution." The library does not establish pro-sandbagging as market standard; both pro- and anti- clauses are in practice and the ABA study tracks the split (`sandbagging.md`).

**Proposed language (anti-sandbagging / disclosed-matters exclusion):**

> Seller shall have no liability under Section 7.1 for any Losses arising from (i) any fact or matter disclosed in the Disclosure Schedules or the data room, or (ii) any matter actually known to Buyer, by name of the individual(s) with actual knowledge, prior to the time of filing the claim. The parties' rights in respect of the matters disclosed on Schedule 4.12 are exclusively as provided in Section 4.12A.

**Why.** Library rule: a seller who discloses a known issue, then gives a clean rep subject to a pro-sandbagging clause, "has effectively agreed to indemnify for the disclosed issue"; the protections are an anti-sandbagging clause, a schedule exception, or a capped special indemnity (`sandbagging.md`; *Akorn v. Fresenius* (Del. Ch. 2018) (dicta) is the library's only case and it is dicta — cite with care). Our package combines (ii) schedule exception + (iii) special indemnity, so (c) as drafted only adds risk. If the buyer refuses the "actual knowledge" bar, minimum position is clause (i) — disclosed matters cannot be "breaches" of a rep that is expressly qualified "except as set forth on Schedule 4.12."

## §7.4(d) Survival — note (not in redline list)

18 months general is inside the 12-24-month market band (`baskets_caps.md`) — keep; the statute-plus-60-days tail for §4.12/taxes moves with the special indemnity, and the general items should not inherit that tail.

## §8.2 Non-Competition — **CHANGE (against Ray's instinct)**

**Proposed language:**

> Seller and Ray Brightline shall not, for five (5) years after Closing, own, manage, operate or provide custom cabinetry fabrication or installation services to customers located within the Trade Area, meaning Travis County and the contiguous Texas counties of Williamson, Hays, Bastrop and Comal. The parties agree this covenant is ancillary to the sale of the goodwill of the Business. If a court of competent authority finds the remaining period or area unenforceable, the covenant shall be reformed and enforced to the maximum extent enforceable.

**Why.** 7 years / 500 miles around Austin for a single-shop custom cabinetry business is "likely overbroad as to both" time and area; reformation under §15.51(c) is the remedy, and "3-5 years within the trade area is typical" (`tx_noncompete_sale_of_business.md`: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50; *Marsh USA v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011)). Ray says sign whatever — but the library's warning is the reason not to: an overbroad covenant to which a material share of the price is allocated "invites IRS scrutiny of the allocation as well" (same file). The county-band choice is a drafting judgment, not a legal requirement; the 5-year outer bound is the library's range. Confirm the price allocation before fixing the number (QUESTIONS.md Q1).

## §9.3 Escrow — **KEEP amount/term for general claims; resist extension**

**Proposed language:**

> $310,000 (10% of the Purchase Price) shall be escrowed for 18 months as security for claims under Section 7.1 other than Section 4.12A. [If Buyer requires security for 4.12A:] a separate escrow of up to $[special-indemnity cap] shall secure Section 4.12A claims and be released upon the earlier of resolution of pending claims and expiration of the §4.12A survival period. In no event shall the general escrow be extended beyond 18 months.

**Why.** $310,000 = 10% = the general cap, held 18 months = the general survival: internally consistent, keep it. The risk is the buyer using the §4.12/tax survival tail to hold the whole $310k for years; the fix is a second, smaller, correctly-sized holdback for the special indemnity only. (Escrow sizing percentages beyond "cap ~10%" are not in the library — no market claim made; labeled unverified.)

18 months general is inside the 12-24-month market band (`baskets_caps.md`) — keep; the statute-plus-60-days tail for §4.12/taxes moves with the special indemnity, and the general items should not inherit that tail.

# Reply to buyer's counsel (J. Whitaker)

**Re: Brightline Cabinetry APA — Schedule 3.3, WARN, and §7.4(c)**

## 1. Schedule 3.3 cannot say "None."

Your draft assumes there are no consent issues. The data room (provided to you) shows there are:

- **Hensley Homes Master Supply Agreement (data room §1.1, 38% of revenue).** §18 bars assignment "whether by operation of law, merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise" absent prior written consent, "which may be withheld in its sole discretion," and makes any purported assignment **void**. In an asset sale that language is enforced according to its terms, so closing without consent would leave the largest customer contract void as to the buyer (`anti_assignment_change_of_control.md`: *SQL Solutions v. Oracle*, 1991 WL 626458 (N.D. Cal.); Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§317, 322). Our proposal: Schedule 3.3 lists Hensley and the shop-lease landlord as required consents, seller uses commercially reasonable efforts pre-closing, and receipt **without modification of economic terms** is a mutual closing condition. We will begin the Hensley conversation this week; if Hensley seeks re-trade terms, we should have a pre-agreed mechanism (price adjustment or walk right) rather than a post-signing dispute.
- **Shop lease (data room §3.1).** Landlord consent required, "not to be unreasonably withheld" — listed on Schedule 3.3; being requested immediately.
- **Cascade Builders (data room §1.2).** Assignment permitted to a successor to substantially all assets **upon notice** — no consent needed; we will deliver the written notice as a closing deliverable on a notice schedule.
- **Twenty-two residential contracts (data room §1.3).** Silent on assignment — rights are generally assignable and performance obligations need consent only where personal (Restatement §§317, 322); we will send customer notices and novate where a homeowner contracted for Brightline's personal performance.
- **Spray-booth permit (data room §4.1)** is non-transferable; your client must reapply (City says 30-60 days). That is a timing/closing-sequencing item — our redline adds a signing-time covenant to file and cooperation, since "sign in two weeks" only works if the permit runway starts now.

## 2. WARN — no notice is required, and here is the arithmetic behind it

WARN covers employers of **100+ employees** (excluding part-time) and plant closings/mass layoffs affecting **50+ employees at a single site** (29 U.S.C. §2101(a)(1); 20 C.F.R. §639.3). Brightline has **14 W-2 employees** (data room §2.1). Even if the 9 hourly installers currently paid on 1099s (data room §2.2) are counted as employees for the analysis — which, given the control facts in §2.2, we think is the conservative view — the total is **23**, far below 100. No WARN notice is required, including if your buyer does not hire everyone, and Texas has no mini-WARN statute (`warn_act.md`). So: we confirm headcount is below threshold, with the express caveat that you should not read our confirmation as an endorsement of the 1099 labels — see item 3 and your own successor-liability analysis (buyer-side FLSA successor exposure and Texas UI successor provisions: `worker_classification_tx_irs.md`; Tex. Lab. Code §201.041; 40 TAC §815.134).

## 3. §7.4(c) — our position

Characterizing §7.4(c) as "market-standard knowledge language" is not accurate: the clause preserves buyer recovery **regardless of knowledge, before or after signing** — that is a **pro-sandbagging** clause, and both pro- and anti-sandbagging positions are in practice; neither is simply "market" (ABA Private Target Deal Points Study, per `sandbagging.md`; *Akorn v. Fresenius* (Del. Ch. 2018), cited in our library only as dicta).

You know from the data room that nine installers do not look like contractors: exclusive service, Brightline trucks and tools, daily scheduling, hourly pay, multi-year tenure — that is the employee pattern under the common-law test (IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41, per `worker_classification_tx_irs.md`). We will not give a clean §4.12 representation on a known issue, and we will not accept a pro-sandbagging clause layered onto it; that combination would just be an indemnity for a disclosed fact with a $3.1M cap and a statute-of-limitations tail (your 7.4(b)/(d)), which is off-market for an operational rep (ABA Deal Points Study, per `baskets_caps.md`).

**Our counter-package**, which we think gets your client real protection rather than paper protection:

1. Schedule 4.12 discloses the 1099 arrangement in full; §4.12 is expressly qualified by it (so it cannot be "breached" as to the disclosed facts);
2. a **special indemnity** for pre-closing employment-tax and wage claims tied to those nine individuals, **no basket, negotiated cap (we expect to land in the $150k-200k range once hours/history data is exchanged), survival to the statute of limitations + 60 days**, secured by a separate small holdback — the only exposure structure that actually maps to your client's real risk, since your buyer must reclassify going forward regardless; and
3. deletion of §7.4(c) in favor of an anti-sandbagging / disclosed-matters exclusion.

If your client would rather have the classification issue priced than papered, we are open to that conversation as well.

— Seller's counsel

# Note to Ray — the three things that bite you after closing

Ray — you asked what bites you later. Three things, in order of how much they can cost.

## 1. The nine 1099 installers. Do not sign the "clean" employee rep.

Your installers ride in your trucks, use your tools, take their daily schedule from the foreman, get paid hourly, and work only for you. That is the textbook definition of employees under the IRS test — "1099 forever" is exactly the fact pattern that gets reclassified, and the industry practice doesn't help you at the IRS (worker_classification file in our reference set). The math: your 2025 1099 payments were $612,000; the employer-side payroll tax on that is roughly $612,000 × 7.65% ≈ **$47,000 per year** (that rate isn't in our reference library, so treat it as an estimate), times about three years = **~$140,000+** before overtime, penalties and interest, and before any years older than the average tenure. The buyer's draft has you signing a rep that "everyone is properly classified and all taxes paid" (§4.12), puts that rep under a cap equal to the **entire purchase price** (~$3.1M), keeps it alive for the whole audit period, and adds a clause (§7.4(c)) saying the buyer's knowledge — even from our own data room — doesn't matter. Translation: you'd be pre-agreeing to reimburse them for a problem you already know about, with no cap that matches the problem. And a rep you know is false isn't just an indemnity problem; it can be a fraud claim, which caps don't protect against. **The fix:** we disclose the installers on a schedule, refuse the clean rep, and give them a dedicated indemnity capped around **$150-200k**. That's a manageable number. The draft is a $3.1M number.

## 2. Hensley Homes — 38% of your revenue — has said nothing yet, and their contract says "consent or it's void."

Their agreement (§18) says you can't transfer it in an asset sale — no consent, **void** — and consent is "in their sole discretion," which legally means they can ask for a price cut as the price of signing (anti-assignment file). The buyer's paperwork says "no consent issues." That's wrong, and if you close without the consent and Hensley walks or re-trades, the buyer will come back at you — 38% of the revenue you just sold them. **The fix:** the consent goes on Schedule 3.3 and becomes a closing condition we both live or die by, and we start the Hensley conversation this week, before signing. Two weeks to sign is fine; two weeks is also exactly how long a landlord (lease consent) and the spray-booth permit re-filing (30-60 days) need to start their clocks.

## 3. The "earn-out" is a headline, not money — unless we fix it.

Their draft pays you 40% of EBITDA over $700,000, up to $400,000, with EBITDA "determined by Buyer under Buyer's accounting policies." Two problems. First, the buyer controls the scoreboard: they can load overhead, management fees and integration costs onto the business and the earn-out is zero — courts have let buyers do this when the contract says buyer's policies (Lazard case in our library). Second, the threshold is set at essentially today's number: at 2025's EBITDA of $740k you'd earn 0.40 × (740,000 − 700,000) = **$16,000**; the full $400,000 needs EBITDA of **$1.7 million**, more than double where you are — and their prepared numbers would start closer to $518k. So the "$400k earn-out" you may be pricing your retirement around is realistically **$0-16k** as drafted. **The fix:** hard accounting definition, no buyer overhead or integration charges, audit rights, an outside accountant settles disputes, and it accelerates if they flip the business — or better, we tell them to cut the earn-out and pay it at closing.

## Two smaller things I also fixed (you said you'd "sign whatever" — please don't)

- **Non-compete:** 7 years, 500 miles, for a shop that serves Austin is almost certainly more than a Texas court will enforce, and if a chunk of the sale price is legally booked to a covenant that won't be enforced, it draws attention to the price split — from you (Texas non-compete file). I proposed 5 years, Travis County plus the counties around it. Since you're retiring, it costs you nothing to be reasonable about it.
- **Escrow:** $310k for 18 months matches the standard claims window — fine. I made sure the installer problem can't drag that whole escrow out for years; if they want security for it, it's a second, small holdback at the $150-200k cap.

Everything above is sourced only to our reference library; where a number isn't in the library (the 7.65% rate, penalty periods), I've flagged it as an estimate rather than law.
